title: Lonnie Mack’s Legendary 1958 Flying V ‘Number 7’ Sells for $550,000 - https://www.thebluesmagazine.com/
content:
Lonnie Mack’s legendary 1958 Gibson Flying V, known as “Number 7,” has sold for $550,000 at Heritage Auctions alongside his 1962 Magnatone amplifier and stage strap. Discover the remarkable history of the guitar that helped shape blues-rock, its connection to Stevie Ray Vaughan, and a special video featuring Joe Bonamassa playing the iconic instrument. Lonnie Mack's legendary 1958 Gibson Flying V, known as “Number 7.” Photo: Heritage Auctions / HA.com. One of the most recognizable guitars in blues-rock history has found a new owner. Lonnie Mack’s legendary 1958 Gibson Flying V, known as “Number 7,” sold for $550,000 at Heritage Auctions on October 15, 2026. The historic instrument was offered together with Mack’s 1962 Magnatone Custom 440 amplifier and his stage-worn guitar strap, bringing a remarkable chapter of American music history to the auction block. The price is impressive, but the story behind this instrument reaches far beyond the world of vintage guitar collecting. For more than five decades, Number 7 was closely associated with Lonnie Mack, the pioneering American guitarist whose powerful blend of blues, country, soul and rock and roll helped shape the sound of modern electric guitar music. From the groundbreaking instrumentals “Memphis” and “Wham!” to his later collaborations with Stevie Ray Vaughan, Mack’s guitar became a symbol of an artist who was exploring the possibilities of blues-rock long before the genre had fully established itself. When Gibson introduced the Flying V in 1958, the guitar looked unlike almost anything else on the market. Its dramatic, arrow-shaped body and futuristic design were a striking departure from the more traditional instruments favored by many players of the era. Built from korina wood, the original Flying V was produced in relatively small numbers. Although the design would later become a familiar sight in rock music, its initial commercial success was limited. Lonnie Mack was among the musicians who immediately recognized its possibilities. According to Mack, his instrument was the seventh Flying V to leave Gibson’s production line, earning it the nickname “Number 7.” The guitar, identified in the Heritage Auctions listing by serial number 176051, would remain his primary instrument for almost his entire career. While other guitarists frequently changed instruments, Mack developed a remarkably close association with his Flying V. It appeared on concert stages, television broadcasts, recording sessions and album covers, eventually becoming one of the most recognizable artist-owned electric guitars in American music.           straight from Blues Magazine. No spam — just the good stuff. Number 7 did not always look the way it does today. The instrument originally featured the natural finish associated with Gibson’s early korina Flying Vs. Around 1963, Gibson refinished the guitar in the deep red color that became part of Mack’s visual identity. Another defining feature is its unusual Bigsby vibrato system. To accommodate the vibrato, a metal support was installed between the two wings of the guitar’s distinctive V-shaped body. The modification gave Number 7 an appearance that remains instantly recognizable to guitar enthusiasts. The instrument also carries the marks of a long working life. Heritage Auctions documented a repaired neck, replacement hardware, and other alterations made over the years. Both original PAF humbucking pickups remain installed, according to the auction description. These details are important to the guitar’s history. Number 7 was not an instrument preserved untouched in a case. It was played, transported, repaired and adapted throughout decades of performances and recording sessions. Lonnie Mack emerged as a distinctive force in American popular music during the early 1960s. His breakthrough came in 1963 with an instrumental interpretation of Chuck Berry’s “Memphis.” The recording showcased an exciting combination of precise picking, driving rhythm and expressive electric guitar playing. His follow-up instrumental, “Wham!,” pushed that approach even further. Both recordings became defining moments in Mack’s career and appeared on his debut album, The Wham of That Memphis Man. What made his playing so influential was the way he moved between musical traditions. Country-inspired picking techniques met the emotional phrasing of the blues, while the power and urgency of rock and roll provided a new setting for the electric guitar. Mack was not simply playing faster or louder. His approach helped demonstrate how an instrumental guitarist could combine technical precision with a deeply expressive sound. The pairing of Number 7 with his Magnatone amplifier became central to that musical identity. That same amplifier, a 1962 Magnatone Custom 440, accompanied the guitar in the Heritage Auctions sale, making the lot particularly significant for anyone interested in Mack’s original equipment and sound. For blues guitar enthusiasts, photographs and auction descriptions tell only part of the story. The real fascination comes from hearing an instrument with such a remarkable musical history. In the video below, titled Joe Bonamassa Plays Lonnie Mack’s Legendary 1958 Flying V “Number 7”, blues-rock guitarist Joe Bonamassa plays the historic instrument. The footage offers a special opportunity to see Number 7 in the hands of another accomplished blues guitarist, rather than simply as a valuable collector’s item. Its distinctive Bigsby arrangement, unusual shape and decades of visible wear are all part of the instrument’s character. It is a fitting connection between different generations of blues guitarists, and a reminder that the value of a historic instrument lies not only in its rarity, but also in the music it was created to make. Among the many guitarists who admired Mack’s playing was Stevie Ray Vaughan. Vaughan recognized Mack as an important influence and later played a significant role in bringing his music back to a wider audience. That connection became especially visible in 1985, when Vaughan worked with Mack on the album Strike Like Lightning. The record introduced Mack’s powerful guitar style to listeners who had discovered the blues through a new generation of musicians. For Mack, the album represented an important return to the spotlight. For Vaughan, the collaboration provided an opportunity to work with a musician whose playing had helped influence his own approach to the electric guitar. The relationship between the two artists illustrates the musical legacy of Number 7. Mack’s early recordings helped develop a guitar vocabulary that would continue to influence blues and rock players for decades. His influence was not limited to Vaughan. Heritage Auctions also identifies artists including Jeff Beck, Eric Clapton, Keith Richards and Duane Allman among the musicians influenced by Mack’s work. In 1993, Gibson acknowledged his contribution with a Lonnie Mack Signature Flying V, paying tribute to the guitarist and the instrument that had become inseparable from his identity. Number 7 was offered as lot 85116 during Heritage Auctions’ Vintage Guitars and Musical Instruments Signature Auction on October 15, 2026. The complete lot included the 1958 Gibson Flying V, Mack’s 1962 Magnatone Custom 440 amplifier, his recognizable stage strap and a hard case. Heritage’s official listing confirms the sale date and the contents of the lot. The realized price is displayed on the auction website only to signed-in visitors. Importantly, that figure represents the sale of the complete lot, not a separately established price for the guitar alone. The Mack collection was one of the standout results of the auction. Another major instrument, a 1959 Gibson Les Paul Standard Sunburst, sold for $781,250. According to published auction reports, that result established a record for a vintage guitar without celebrity provenance. While the Les Paul attracted attention for its originality and condition, Mack’s Flying V represented a different kind of historical importance: an instrument closely connected to the musician who helped define its place in popular music. Lonnie Mack died in April 2016, leaving behind an influential catalog of recordings and a lasting reputation as one of the early innovators of blues-rock guitar. His place in music history is closely connected to Number 7. The guitar accompanied him during an era when musicians were discovering new possibilities for electric instruments. It was there during the recordings that established his reputation, remained part of his performances for decades, and became an instantly recognizable symbol of his career. Its distinctive red finish, unusual vibrato system and visible signs of use make it much more than a rare example of Gibson’s early Flying V design. For collectors, the $550,000 sale is a remarkable result. For musicians and blues fans, the instrument represents something that cannot be measured by an auction price: the sound and influence of a guitarist who helped change the course of electric guitar music. And thanks to footage such as Joe Bonamassa’s demonstration, Number 7 can still be appreciated for what made it legendary in the first place — the music. title: Thomson Reuters v. ROSS: Third Circuit Recognizes a Licensing Market for AI Training Data (via Passle) - Baker Botts
content: On September 29, 2026, the Third Circuit issued what appears to be the first federal appellate decision on whether training AI on copyrighted material is fair use. In Thomson Reuters v. ROSS Intelligence, the court affirmed that case-law headnotes are copyrightable and that using them to train a non-generative legal-research tool was not fair use. Early coverage has emphasized footnote 7, which distinguishes AI that "cannot generate original expression" from generative models, and the court's finding that "the evidence shows that the market for licensing headnotes as text to train AI is rapidly developing." Less attention has gone to how courts will test evidence of that market. Under the fourth factor, the court found harm to the original market and to the value of the headnotes, and it also recognized a potential derivative market for licensing them as training data. It cited evidence that the copyright owner was using its headnotes "as training data for its own AI search products" and held that the absence of licenses to third parties "does not disprove that a market exists to do so." Consistent with Warhol, the burden remained on the party asserting fair use. This reasoning is difficult to square with two June 2025 decisions from the Northern District of California. Judge Alsup assumed that a market for licensing books as training data could develop but held that it "is not one the Copyright Act entitles Authors to exploit." Judge Chhabria held that whether such a market "exists or is likely to develop is irrelevant," because counting lost licensing fees for a transformative use as market harm would make the fourth factor circular. The Third Circuit did not address circularity, although it had already concluded that the use was "minimally transformative, at best." Read together, the decisions may suggest that the first factor operates as a threshold. If a court finds the training use transformative, licensing evidence may be legally irrelevant under the California approach; if it does not, that evidence may decide the fourth factor. Where courts do weigh licensing evidence, the analysis may resemble a reasonable royalty dispute in a patent case. Courts may have to decide whether a proffered license is comparable to the use at issue, whether a bundled deal reflects a price for training at all, and how much weight to give a license negotiated to settle litigation. The Federal Circuit has held that licenses used to set a royalty must be "commensurate with what the defendant has appropriated" and has cautioned that "litigation itself can skew the results of the hypothetical negotiation" (ResQNet). In EcoFactor, the court held under Rule 702 that a damages expert should not have been allowed to testify that prior licenses reflected a per-unit royalty the licenses themselves did not support. The Supreme Court used similar reasoning in Google v. Oracle, giving little weight under the fourth factor to licensing negotiations that "concerned much more than 37 packages of declaring code." AI fair use cases may see the same comparability disputes and Rule 702 challenges to licensing experts. The analogy has limits: the burden of proof runs the other way, and patent law has no equivalent to the circularity concern. For companies on either side of a training-data deal, the practical takeaway is that license terms may become evidence in fair use litigation. Companies should watch whether further review takes up the circularity question, whether the next district court follows the Third Circuit, and whether courts begin testing these licenses the way patent courts test comparable licenses. title: 'Just a Flat-Out Lie': Collins Says She Couldn't Have Known Kavanaugh Would Vote to Overturn Roe v. Wade - Common Dreams

Susan Collins (R-Maine) speaks to reporters as she arrives for the Senate Republicans’ lunch in the US Capitol on September 30, 2026. As she faces a tough reelection fight in Maine, Republican Sen. Susan Collins is twisting the facts about her role in laying the groundwork for the US Supreme Court’s overturning of abortion rights. Throughout the campaign, Collins has been dogged by questions about her fateful decision in 2018 to cast a key vote to confirm Justice Brett Kavanaugh to the court. In 2022, he joined the court’s conservative majority to overturn the 1973 Roe v. Wade precedent, allowing states to impose severe new bans and restrictions on abortion. In June, Collins—who has described herself as pro-choice—said she did “not regret” her vote to confirm Kavanaugh, falsely claiming that Roe was overturned by a 6-3 margin and was therefore doomed regardless of her vote. In fact, the precedent was overturned by a 5-4 margin, meaning Kavanaugh’s vote proved decisive. Now in a dead heat race with Democratic nominee Troy Jackson, who has repeatedly hammered her on abortion rights, Collins has continued to defend her confirmation vote. She’s also kept fudging the truth. “I’m very disappointed in his vote to overturn Roe v. Wade,” Collins said of Kavanaugh during an interview published Monday by Maine ABC affiliate WMTW. “There was no way for me to anticipate that.” Collins had, in fact, been warned that Kavanaugh might overturn Roe v. Wade. In her October 5, 2018, speech supporting his confirmation, she explicitly acknowledged “the concern that Judge Kavanaugh would seek to overturn Roe v. Wade” and noted that President Donald Trump had pledged to nominate judges who would do so. Reproductive freedom advocates cautioned her that Kavanaugh was not being truthful when he said he considered Roe to be settled precedent, citing his history of ruling against abortion access and praising former Chief Justice William Rehnquist’s dissent in Roe. But Collins dismissed these advocates’ warnings, arguing that Republican-appointed Justices Sandra Day O’Connor, David Souter, and Anthony Kennedy had voted to reaffirm Roe despite opposition to some of their nominations from abortion rights groups. “Suffice it to say, prominent advocacy organizations have been wrong,” Collins said. In this case, they were not. Lisa Margulies, spokesperson for Planned Parenthood Votes in Maine, said it was dishonest of Collins to plead innocence. “It’s just a flat-out lie that Susan Collins had ‘no way’ of knowing Brett Kavanaugh would overturn our federal right to abortion,” she said. “Mainers drove down to DC and begged her not to confirm him. They knew he was a direct threat to abortion, and so did Susan Collins.” “This is just another flimsy attempt to avoid responsibility for her actions,” Margulies said. “Enough is enough. title: Little v. Llano County (5th Circuit 2025) - Free Speech Center
content: Home » Articles » Case » Book Banning and Libraries » Little v. Llano County (5th Circuit 2025) The 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in 2025 overturned an injunction against a public library in Llano County, Texas, from removing books based on complaints of seven library patrons, rejecting that other patrons had a right to receive information. The majority opinion reasoned that the decision about what to put in public library collections was a form of government speech and could not be subject to a First Amendment challenge. (Photo, iStock illustration) This case deals with the right of public libraries to withdraw books from circulation. The case arose when seven library patrons sued the librarian and other officials for removing 17 books from the Llano County, Texas, public library, guided in part by a list of offensive books that a state legislator had identified. Relying in part on the Supreme Court’s ambiguous decision regarding school libraries in Board of Education, Island Trees Union Free School District v. Pico (1982), a U.S. district court had issued a preliminary injunction ordering the books to be restored and prohibiting the withdrawal of other books. In a decision in Little v. Llano County, 103 F.4th 1140 (2024), the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit had largely upheld this injunction on the basis that patrons had a right to receive information, albeit in a ruling that had elicited a strong dissent. The 2025 decision described in this entry by the court sitting en banc overturned that injunction on the grounds that the “right to receive information” was an improper basis for challenging the removal of books and that library collection decisions constituted a form of “government speech,” which is not subject to First Amendment challenge. The majority opinion, representing 10 members of the 5th Circuit court was authored by Judge Stuart Kyle Duncan, who had authored a blistering dissent in the court’s earlier decision. In the introduction to his decision, Judge Duncan emphasized that he was not sanctioning book banning. Taking issue with a decision by the 8th Circuit court in GLBT Youth in Iowa Schools Task Force v. Reynolds, 114 F.4th 660 (2024), the judge also argued that the government was not speaking “through the words of the books themselves,” but “by selecting some books over others and presenting that collection to the public—just as a museum does when it curates a collection of various schools of art.” After reviewing a number of cases based on the right to receive information, including Stanley v. Georgia (1969) [involving the right to view pornography in one’s home], Duncan observed that although the cases established that the government’s power to prevent one person from receiving another’s speech, “In none of these cases . . . did a plaintiff invoke a right to receive information from the government.” They thus represented a negative right against government interference rather than a positive right on the part of the government, he said. Citing Muir v. Alabama Educ. Television Comm’n, 688 F.2d 1033 (Former 5th Cir. 1982), Duncan argued that the Supreme Court’s decision in Pico was so fractured that it had no precedential value. While other circuit court decisions had addressed the issue of whether “a library could evict someone from its premises, it had not ruled that “someone could demand the library put certain books on its shelves.” Duncan argued that “if people can challenge which books libraries remove, they can challenge which books library buys,” which he thought was far beyond judicial purview.  More generally, he argued that judicial attempts to decide which books were appropriate and which were not “would tie courts in endless knots.” Because a library is not a warehouse, it has no obligation to keep books that are “out-of-date, inaccurate, biased, vulgar, lurid, or silly.” Acknowledging that libraries were exercising viewpoint discrimination, Duncan pointed out that those who could not find a book they wanted in a library could borrow or buy a copy or go to another library to find it. Duncan accordingly decided that the 5th Circuit’s decision in Campbell v. St. Tammany Parish School Board, 64 F.3d 184 (1994), prohibiting the removal of the book “Voodoo & Hoodoo” from a school library had been “wrongly decided” and was accordingly overruled. Returning to the issue of government speech, Duncan pointed to numerous precedents, most notably City of Pleasant Grove v. Summum (2009) [accepting a monument on government grounds] and United States v. American Library Association (2003) [accepting age filters on library internet access] where the government had to decide which speech to permit and exclude on its premises. Libraries have the right and the duty to curate their collections. Duncan further argued that a library did not create a public forum by selecting books. Even when libraries created a limited public forum by opening its premises to expressive activities, it was not required to open its bookshelves to everything. In further considering the case of Shurtleff v. City of Boston (2022) [ruling that a city that allowed private parties to fly their flags on government property created a limited public forum], Duncan reviewed the long history of public libraries and long-established criteria for curating such collections by excluding volumes that were biased, racist, inaccurate, or outdated. Duncan thus argued that the 8th Circuit Court had been mistaken in GLBT Youth in Iowa Schools Task Force v. Reynolds, 114 F.4th 660 (2024), in ruling that the public would not view the placement and removal of books in public schools as government speech. Judge James C. Ho issued a concurring opinion, which emphasized that the founders “enact a charter of negative liberties,” or “freedom from, not freedom to.” He also argued that if the government was not required to buy certain books, then it could hardly be forbidden from removing them. Although plaintiffs had the “right to read books,” Ho said that “They don’t have a First Amendment right to force a public library to provide them.” Judge Stephen A. Higginson wrote a dissenting opinion on behalf of seven justices. Higginson went into considerable detail in describing the actions that led to this suit, arguing that the reasons that officials had given for removing books was largely pretextual and was based on their dislike of their viewpoints and contents. Higginson believed that Pico, Campbell, and other decisions had pointed to “the right to receive information and the right to be free from officially prescribed orthodoxy,” which he thought the library had tried to enforce in this case. Whereas Duncan had pointed to disagreements in how to apply the Pico-Campbell standard, Higginson did not believe that its principle had proved to be unworkable or had invited greater confusion than in other areas of jurisprudence. He also thought that if Pico were overruled, this should be the job of the U.S. Supreme Court. Arguing that the majority opinion had been too flippant and dismissive of First Amendment rights, Higginson said that the real issue was “whether government officials may restrict—abridge—the spectrum of ideas available to the public by culling books from library shelves, simply because those officials find the books’ ideas inappropriate, offensive, or otherwise undesirable,” to which he answered with a resounding “No.” Favorably citing some examples, he did say that “public libraries . . . are free to organize their books in a manner that ensures patrons are directed to age-appropriate materials.” John R. This past weekend, Michie Stadium celebrated an Army victory over Florida Atlantic University, accepted two reunion gift presentations, and welcomed the newest member of the Army Mule Team. Together, these milestones reflected the ongoing momentum for the progress of West Point’s programs, facilities, and cadets. In celebration of its 20th reunion, the West Point Class of 2006 presented a $725,000 reunion gift supporting both Goethals Hall and the West Point Press. The gift, presented by Class President Brandon Archuleta and classmate Sam Russo, establishes a new record for the largest 20th-reunion gift in Academy history. The Class of 2016 also marked a reunion milestone with a $300,000 gift in celebration of its 10th reunion. Presented by Class President EJ Coleman and Class Vice President Jake Tyer, the gift to Goethals Hall and the Modern War Institute marks the class’s first reunion gift to West Point. Both class gifts advance the Academy’s academic and military missions and create continued opportunities for cadets to learn, lead, and prepare for future service. Scheduled to welcome its first classes in January 2027, Goethals Hall will house the Departments of Mechanical & Aerospace Engineering, Civil & Environmental Engineering, Electrical Engineering & Computer Science, and Systems Engineering. The state-of-the-art facility honors Major General George Washington Goethals, Class of 1880, the Army engineer who supervised the construction and opening of the Panama Canal. The Modern War Institute connects academic study with the challenges of contemporary conflict. Recently, it hosted the Class of 2006 Modern War Conference, centered on “Deterrence in the Pacific.” Military, defense, and national security experts joined cadets for five panels exploring strategic competition in the Indo-Pacific, deterrence, future warfare, and the U.S. Army’s role in the region. These transformational gifts to the Margin of Excellence provide resources and opportunities that enrich the cadet experience beyond what federal funding alone can provide. The weekend also included an on-field recognition of Steve Townes ’75, who presented Ranger V, the newest member of the Army Mule Team. The Army mules are a cherished West Point icon, embodying the traditions and spirit of the Academy. Ranger V is only the third female mule to join the century-old program. Her distinctive dunskin coloring adds a new look to the team, giving the Army Mule Team its own version of black and gold. Since 2001, Steve and Suzy Townes have endowed the Army Mule Program, providing resources to sustain the team in perpetuity. Their generosity helps preserve the mule as a living symbol of the West Point brand, embodying the strength, resilience, and steadfastness associated with the Academy while maintaining its familiar presence at Army athletic events and Academy celebrations. These moments reflect the Long Gray Line’s commitment to leadership that extends well beyond the uniform. Through the generosity of alumni, friends of the Academy, and dedicated benefactors, West Point’s mission and traditions remain strong, providing future generations of cadets with opportunities to develop into the leaders of character our nation requires. 698 Mills Road

title: INTERVIEW: Dei V Serves Up New Sides of His Sound on ‘Flavorz Pack’ - Remezcla
content: Dei V dishes up Flavorz Pack, a 17-track studio album that builds on his iconic Flavorz brand and invites listeners to savor his music in a new way. The album unfolds in four parts: licorice, chocolate, paleta, and a special bonus track featuring Rauw Alejandro titled “All Night”—showcasing the Puerto Rican artist’s diverse sonic palette. Each part reveals a different side of Dei V. Licorice welcomes listeners into the Flavorz Pack universe with his signature trap flow. Staying true to his roots, he blends trap and hip-hop into a gritty, raw sound that’s unmistakably his own. Meanwhile, chocolate reveals a softer, more sensual side as he trades his classic malianteo sound for romantiqueo. With paleta, he keeps things sleek and finely tuned, exploring playful R&B influences that further showcase his versatility. On release day, Dei V was taking it all in. On his way to the barber in Miami, he spoke with Remezcla about what the album means to him. “I think there was something I still needed to do with Flavorz, which is one of my brands. I released the first EP, Los Flavorz, but I hadn’t released a full-length album for fans. I’ve been taking some time to rest and be a dad, but I wanted to come back strong. I feel like the music I’m releasing now defines me. I feel like I’m a more mature Dei V. I also think the music has leveled up.” Since his 2023 breakthrough project ¿ Quién es Dei V?, the Puerto Rican artist has steadily cemented his place in Latin trap. The project’s title drew inspiration from a viral video in which a woman asked who Dei V was, seemingly intending to disparage him. Instead, the moment became a turning point in his career, sparking public interest and earning him support from fellow artists. Collaborations with Myke Towers and Jay Wheeler followed, along with a feature on Karol G’s MAÑANA SERA BONITO album through the track “Gatita Gangster.” Today, Dei V collaborates with some of Latin music’s biggest names. Most recently, he joined Bad Bunny and Omar Courtz on “VeLDÁ,” a standout track from Debí Tirar Más Fotos, which has achieved global success and become his first song to surpass a billion streams. Having benefited from the support and co-signs that helped propel his career, Dei V is now extending that opportunity to emerging artists. Flavorz Pack brings newcomers Xaed and Galeno into the mix alongside heavy hitters Rauw Alejandro, Wisin, Myke Towers, Kendo Kaponi, Ozuna, and Nicky Jam. Dei V is determined to show listeners that his artistry extends beyond any one genre or sound. “I want people to understand that I’m an artist who can make all kinds of music. I’ll always surprise them and give it my all. With every project, I learn a little more about how to put together an album and create a body of work.” That intention runs through Flavorz Pack. From its distinct sonic chapters to its carefully considered details, the project reflects his desire to offer listeners something beyond the expected. As Dei V explains, “Overall, I feel like music has become monotonous.” With Flavorz Pack, he pushes against that monotony, approaching the album as a complete listening experience rather than simply a collection of tracks. Ultimately, Flavorz Pack presents Dei V as a multidimensional artist who keeps refining his sound while taking pride in what he delivers to fans. He’s taking his time, embracing his growth, and making music on his own terms. Above all, he says he “simply wanted to use this project to let them [fans] know that I haven’t gone anywhere, and I’m not going anywhere. We’re going to keep making music that’s better than before and keep putting in the work, just like we always have.” This site is protected by reCAPTCHA and Google Privacy Policy and the Terms of service. title: Back-to-back for Lady Dolphins in v-ball - Marianas Press
content: The Marianas High School Lady Dolphins swam their way to a repeat title of the PSS-NMIVA Girls High School Volleyball League after they beat Grace Christian Academy Lady Eagles in straight sets this 2026-2027 season, 21-14, 21-18, in front of their home crowd on Thursday, Oct. 8. Climbing through the ranks in the playoffs, the Lady Dolphins came out unscathed despite a rocky regular season. On the last day of the playoffs, they first defeated MCS, 21-18, 21-8; then beat Saipan International School, 21-7, 21-11; and finally, after a break, they faced off against GCA in the finals. GCA, who defeated MHS in the regular season, came out strong with well placed hits and strong serves. But, the Lady Dolphins created less errors and moved as one, having more chemistry than they did in the beginning of the season. The first set was a quick one in favor of MHS, 21-14. The second set had more battles at the net and it was a tight one in the beginning. MHS’ defense at the back stood their ground though, digging and bumping as much as they could. GCA was their own worst enemy, with errors on the returns, until eventually MHS sealed the deal, 21-18. The MHS team included Erika Zandueta, Ella Hall, Lina Tsukagoshi, Hiromi Sasamoto, Rhodalyn Zandueta, Jana Agbuya, Emma Sablan, Genicia Agulto, Mia Guerrero, Dana Munar, Kylie Leomo, Mary Joyce Anover, Czarina Valdez, Maya Taga, and Mailee Santos. GCA’s roster consisted of Anne Arriola, Venice Camaisa, Maria Sofia Gomez, Liyanna Libut, Breanna Lopez, Misako Ota, Eliane Pagaduan, Princess Siapno, Joanella Yarofalir, and Yu Xuan (Breanna) Zheng. Zandueta and Hall, who are both seniors, were happy that they got to repeat as champions. Hall, a middle hitter, said, “Before we started our streak, another school had a very long streak, so it feels good that we get to keep it.” MHS defeated SSHS in last season’s finals, while GCA had an 8-year championship streak before that. For Zandueta, an outside hitter, she said, “Considering all the circumstances that were happening in Agape [Gym], we had a chance to build our way up in the playoffs this season. Having the championships in our home court felt easier than playing at Agape in my opinion.” Hall added, “I feel like also because of the losses in the past games, we pinpointed what was wrong, and we worked on it together as a team and I feel like it made the difference.” When asked if there was a doubt that they could retain their title, Hall said, “I had a little bit of doubt, but I still had confidence in my team. I knew that we were going to do good.” Meanwhile, Zandueta said, “I didn’t have doubts. I knew we were going to win this. I wanted this so bad like as a senior—our last year playing, I wanted this so bad.” They then gave shoutouts to their family, teammates, coaches, and principals that came out to support them throughout the season. Third place went to Mount Carmel School Lady Knights after defeating Saipan Southern High School in three tough sets, 15-21, 22-20, 15-12.

title: SpacemiT Launches 46-Core V100 RISC‑V Server CPU - markets.businessinsider.com
content:
Shenzhen, Oct.  20, 2026  (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- SpacemiT has introduced the V100, a 46-core RISC‑V server CPU designed for general-purpose data center computing, AI agent infrastructure and AI acceleration. Announced at RISC‑V Summit China 2026, the processor launches alongside three server platforms for compute, AI and storage workloads. Speaking at the summit, RISC‑V International CEO Andrea Gallo highlighted the architecture’s growing role in AI computing and data centers. “RISC‑V supports AI training and inference in data centers,” he said. “RISC‑V is the architecture for intelligent computing.” According to SpacemiT, V100 is the industry’s first general-purpose processor to fully comply with the RISC‑V server specifications, with native support for mainstream server operating systems and virtualization stacks. Its implementation covers the RVA23 Profile, the RISC‑V Server SoC and Server Platform specifications, Boot and Runtime Services (BRS), and the RISC‑V Security Model. The company says V100 has passed all BRS compliance tests and allows users to install, boot and run mainstream Linux distributions directly on V100 systems. “V100 is an important step for SpacemiT as we expand from devices to the cloud,” said Zhijian Chen, the company’s founder and CEO. “It also reflects RISC‑V’s progress toward real-world data center deployments at scale.” Introduced jointly by SpacemiT and the XiangShan team, V100 combines six XiangShan Kunminghu V2R2 cores with 40 of SpacemiT’s own X100 cores. The heterogeneous 46-core design supports clock speeds of up to 2.4 GHz, while a cache-coherent interconnect enables dual-socket configurations with up to 92 cores. Each processor supports eight DDR5 memory channels and 52 PCIe 5.0 lanes for connecting AI accelerators, high-speed network adapters and storage devices. V100 provides hardware-assisted CPU, interrupt and I/O virtualization. SpacemiT says the platform works with upstream Linux KVM without requiring a custom kernel. The chip also includes a hardware root of trust and server-class reliability, availability and serviceability (RAS) features. The accompanying systems are the C2201 computing server, G5201 intelligent computing server and S5236 storage server, targeting general-purpose computing, AI acceleration and large-scale data storage, respectively. The G5201 accommodates eight full-height, full-length, double-width accelerator cards. SpacemiT says it has validated the system with accelerators from Kunlunxin and other vendors. The server also supports RDMA (remote direct memory access) networking for high-speed clusters. SpacemiT is supplying server motherboard reference designs, firmware, baseboard management controller (BMC) support and hardware design documentation to help system builders develop servers under their own brands. SpacemiT says Ubuntu 26.10 officially supports V100. Its work on processor support and toolchain optimization has also been merged into upstream open-source projects, including the Linux kernel and LLVM. The company is working with Canonical, the RISE Project and Scaleway to give open-source developers access to RVA23-compatible hardware, contributing K3 compute clusters to shared development infrastructure. SpacemiT also sponsored DebConf26 in Argentina, supported Debian community testing on the K3 platform and co-organized the Physical AI Hackathon in Hong Kong for developers worldwide. Partners including DeepComputing and Banana Pi are bringing K3-based products to international markets. These include mainboards for Framework modular laptops, development boards and compute modules. SpacemiT says international customers have placed orders for both K3 chips and K3-based cluster servers. In 2026, the company has participated in Open Source Summit and Embedded Linux Conference North America; Ubuntu Summit in London; RISC‑V Summit Europe in Italy; and Linux Plumbers Conference and Open Source Summit Europe in Prague. Its presentations and demonstrations have covered high-performance RISC‑V computing, operating system support, on-device AI and upstream open-source development. At the AI for Good Global Summit in Geneva, SpacemiT’s Emotional Companion Robot was featured in the Innovate for Impact collection of case studies. The company also demonstrated K3-based on-device AI applications at the Global Innovation Show (GIS) in Hong Kong. With K1, K3 and now V100, SpacemiT is extending its product family across devices, edge systems and data centers. Its longer-term strategy brings together processor design, system software, complete systems and international partnerships to build a business around open-architecture computing. SpacemiT designs general-purpose processors based on the RISC‑V instruction set architecture. Headquartered in Beijing, the company has R&D centers in Hangzhou, Shanghai, Shenzhen and Zhuhai. Its team has extensive experience in CPU architecture, chip development and high-volume production and delivery. The company’s K1, K3 and V100 processor lineup spans devices, edge systems and data centers. SpacemiT develops processors, system software and complete hardware platforms to bring RISC‑V products into volume deployment. It also invests in operating system support, virtualization, compiler toolchains and open-source software, working with developers and industry partners worldwide to make the open RISC‑V ISA a foundation for future digital infrastructure. title: Gibson Reveals Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers Flying V Guitars - Rock & Blues Muse
content:
Gibson Reveals Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers Flying V Guitars Gibson honors that extraordinary legacy with a limited-edition 50th Anniversary Tom Petty Flying V™ guitar inspired by the iconic Heartbreakers logo featured on the band’s self-titled 1976 debut album. Known collectively as the “Flying Five,” the collection comprises five distinctive gloss nitrocellulose lacquer finishes, with only 50 guitars produced in each color worldwide. The Tom Petty Flying V 50th Anniversary guitars and apparel are available worldwide now at Gibson Garage locations and at www.gibson.com. Offered in Gainesville Gold, Graphite Metallic, Heartbreaker Red, Pearl White Metallic, and Pelham Blue, the Tom Petty Flying V is limited to 250 guitars worldwide. A new assortment of Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers-inspired apparel, accessories, and collectibles launches alongside the guitars, giving musicians and fans new ways to celebrate the band’s music, style, and enduring independent spirit. The Gibson launch joins a landmark season of albums, special events, and anniversary celebrations from the band and the Tom Petty estate. Above (L-R): The limited-edition Tom Petty Flying V™ arrives in Heartbreaker Red, Gainesville Gold, Pelham Blue, Graphite Metallic, and Pearl White Metallic; with only 250 guitars available worldwide. Inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2002, Tom Petty’s legacy as a songwriter, performer, and storyteller remains as powerful as ever. Across five decades, the music of Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers has embodied freedom, resilience, independence, and uncompromising American rock ’n’ roll, proving that authentic artistry, unforgettable songwriting, and masterful musicianship never go out of style. The anniversary celebration also includes the Nov. 6 release of Origins 1971–1978, a box set from the Tom Petty Estate tracing Petty’s early recording career through the formation and early years of the Heartbreakers. The collection pairs rare, live, and previously unreleased recordings with the band’s first two albums. “The Heartbreakers logo has been part of the band’s identity since the first album, so seeing Gibson reinterpret it through the Flying V 50th anniversary edition feels overdue as they have been part of the story since the beginning. The V was an essential part of the imagery onstage for my dad as well as the band rose to fame in the 1970’s,” says Adria Petty. “The collection honors Tom and the Heartbreakers’ history while giving musicians and fans a new way to carry that spirit forward.” “Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers have meant so much to so many, with timeless songs that continue to inspire us today,” adds Beth Heidt, Chief Marketing Officer at Gibson. “It is a profound honor to celebrate 50 years of that music through these instruments and this collection. Every Flying V and every piece of the apparel collection carries that incredible spirit forward, connecting with the fans who have loved them all along and the next generation ready to make these songs their own.” Built with a resonant mahogany Flying V body and matching mahogany neck, the Tom Petty Flying V 50th Anniversary pairs the unmistakable silhouette of Gibson’s radical classic with details rooted in Heartbreakers history. Its fast-playing SlimTaper™ neck and rosewood fretboard—with a 12-inch radius, 22 medium jumbo frets, and acrylic dot inlays—support effortless chording, expressive bends, and long nights onstage. A mother-of-pearl Gibson logo crowns the headstock, while Grover® Rotomatic® tuners and a Graph Tech® nut provide dependable tuning stability. A Heartbreaker 50th truss rod cover and a reproduction of Tom Petty’s signature on the back of the headstock make every instrument an unmistakable commemorative piece. Each guitar ships in a Gibson hardshell case. The five gloss nitrocellulose lacquer finishes give the “Flying Five” distinct personalities: Gainesville Gold brings celebratory warmth; Graphite Metallic adds a sleek, stage-ready edge; Heartbreaker Red delivers bold rock ’n’ roll impact; Pearl White Metallic offers luminous contrast; and Pelham Blue channels vintage Gibson cool. Beneath the finish, a pair of 70s Tribute humbucker™ pickups moves from clear, articulate cleans to muscular, arena-ready drive. Hand-wired electronics include individual volume controls, a master tone control with an Orange Drop® capacitor, and a three-way pickup selector. Gold-plated hardware—including an aluminum Nashville Tune-O-Matic™ bridge and Stop Bar tailpiece—joins Gold Top Hat knobs, a three-ply white pickguard, and a cream toggle switch cap for a look that is both celebratory and unmistakably Gibson. With only 50 guitars produced in each color, every finish is equally rare. Read more about the Gibson Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers 50th Anniversary Collection on the Gibson Gazette HERE. title: The 2027 Ford Ranger Might Be Gaining a Dose of Raptor-Like Power - Road & Track
content: Ford’s twin-turbocharged 3.0-liter V-6 could be headed to the regular Ranger, bringing 380 horsepower and 440 pound-feet of torque with it. If you're shopping for a new Ford Ranger, there are plenty of reasons to consider stepping up to the Ranger Raptor: Fox 2.5-inch Live Valve shocks, a Watts-link rear suspension with trailing arms, and beefy 33-inch tires, just to name a few—and then there's the potent 3.0-liter EcoBoost twin-turbo V-6 pumping out 405 horsepower and 430 pound-feet of torque. That's a pretty compelling package, but what if you want the power without all the off-road hardware? Well, for 2027, you might be able to get pretty darn close. According to our colleagues at Car and Driver, citing a report from Autoevolution, a reportedly leaked 2027 Ranger order guide suggests that the available 2.7-liter V-6 could be replaced by a twin-turbocharged 3.0-liter V-6. The 2.3-liter turbocharged four-cylinder, making 270 horsepower, would remain the standard engine in non-Raptor Ranger models. Ford hasn't announced output figures for the rumored 3.0-liter, but if it receives the same tune as the 2027 Bronco that ditches the 2.7-liter six-pot for the 3.0-liter version, it could produce 380 horsepower and 440 pound-feet of torque. The new 3.0-liter V-6 will reportedly be available in 2027 XLT and Lariat 4x4 models. If the report is accurate, the 2027 Ranger XLT and Lariat would have just 25 fewer horsepower than the saurian Ranger, while actually producing 10 additional pound-feet of torque. Check the box for the new engine, add the FX4 Off-Road Package, and you could have something resembling a budget Raptor. Of course, just how much of a bargain that would be remains to be seen. For 2026, the available 2.7-liter V-6 is a $4045 option on the XLT, with the required XLT High package and $2295 on the Lariat. There's no pricing information yet for the rumored 3.0-liter. The engine may be the big news, but the 2027 Ford Ranger is also expected to receive a few other tweaks as well. New wheel designs and revised grille finishes for the XLT and Lariat trims are expected, and the color palette is reportedly getting a shakeup as well, with Neptune Blue replacing Velocity Blue and Carbonized Gray disappearing from the lineup. On the inside, Ford is supposedly retiring the Sandstone interior color in favor of a new shade called Space Gray. The entry-level XL is reported to gain some welcome upgrades: the current 10.1-inch touchscreen will allegedly give way to a larger 12.0-inch display, while dual-zone automatic climate control supposedly becomes standard equipment. Of course, none of this is official until Ford makes an announcement. Road & Track has reached out to Ford for confirmation, and will let you know if we receive a response; but if the rumored engine upgrade becomes reality, the 2027 Ranger could offer an appealing alternative for buyers who want Raptor-like power without the Raptor's price tag. title: Trademark case: Weems Industries, Inc. v. Teknor Apex Co., USA - Wolters Kluwer
content: Trademark case: Weems Industries, Inc. v. Teknor Apex Co., USA The court upheld findings that color served a safety function and that case qualified as exceptional under the Lanham Act. The Eighth Circuit affirmed a district court judgment canceling Weems Industries' registered trademark for the chartreuse color used on its water hoses, concluding that the color is a functional product feature that cannot be protected as a trademark. The appeals court also upheld an award of more than $3 million in attorney fees to competitor Teknor Apex, agreeing that the litigation qualified as an exceptional case under the Lanham Act. Because the court affirmed on functionality grounds, it did not reach the district court's separate finding that the color lacked acquired distinctiveness (Weems Industries, Inc. v. Teknor Apex Co., No. 24-3608 (8th Cir. Jul. 30, 2026)).
