title: All the dumb moments that make this title so much sweeter: Part V (2020-26) - Posting and Toasting
content: In the end, all of this was worth it for the climb to the top. It’s Opening Night. The Knicks will play meaningful basketball tonight for the first time in four months. But, more importantly, they will see the fruits of their labor realized. They will receive their championship rings from Commissioner Adam Silver and watch as a new championship banner is raised at Madison Square Garden to hang for the rest of eternity. Add Posting and Toasting as a preferred source to see more of our reporting on Google. Maybe the gravity of what they’ve done will be fully realized as they watch it raised to the ceiling. Maybe the weight of 53 years of pain and misery can finally leave their shoulders too, if it hasn’t already. Over the last few weeks, I’ve spent the preseason recounting the horrid details of the 53-year drought. All the moments when we were ashamed of our team. All the moments when it hurt to be a Knicks fan. All the moments that made the championship drought really sting more and more. If you want to read all of this at once, for some reason, here’s the other four parts before we get into it: When we last left off, the world was mired in the COVID-19 pandemic. The Knicks had a new executive in Leon Rose, who would soon hire a new culture-changing coach, Tom Thibodeau. Together, they were tasked with first breaking the cycle of mediocrity and humiliation that had plagued the franchise for 20 years, and once they accomplished that, they were tasked with somehow ending the near-five-decade drought that seemed like an impenetrable cloud around the franchise. What’s different about this part is that there are very few (if any) front-office decisions or real drama. The Leon Rose era has been as drama-free as any executive tenure in basketball history, and none of his moves have been as head-scratching as some in the past. Did some age terribly? Absolutely, but we can’t call picking Obi Toppin or signing Evan Fournier and Kemba Walker a traditionally “dumb” move when everyone was excited about it. The benefit of it being so recent is hindsight. Instead, it’s all in-game experiences. The highs and lows. The injuries. The playoff heartbreak. The slow rise from plucky underdog to dominant champion. Sit back and enjoy. None of this can hurt you anymore. Since we’re only covering the bad moments, we’re going to be jumping around a bit here, starting with that magical 2021 season. I’ll get into it more in a bit, but the Knicks emerged out of nowhere to go from a perennial loser to an actual playoff team over the course of the 2020-21 season. It was a smattering of unlikely heroes along the way that made it so special. There were some bad subplots to the season, though, namely with Mitchell Robinson. Back when he wasn’t the only homegrown Knick, Robinson dealt with his first challenging series of injuries in 2020-21. In early February, while he was firmly establishing himself as a foundational big man, he fractured his fourth metacarpal in his right hand. He missed 15 games and returned in mid-March, but it would only last four games before he came down awkwardly on his right foot while on defense against the Bucks on March 27. A fractured fifth metatarsal in his foot ended his season. It would be a gigantic blow to a Knicks team who was sitting at a competitive 24-22 and firmly in the playoff hunt. While they survived and even thrived with Nerlens Noel and Taj Gibson down the stretch, they would miss their young big in the playoffs. That season truly was magical. A ragtag group of misfit toys, from journeyman veterans to underperforming young guys, all stepped up en route to a 41-31 season that brought hope and belief back to a city that was hit harder by COVID-19 than any in the U.S. An incredible regular season saw them go 41-31 and take the No. 4 seed. That meant home-court advantage in the first playoff series at Madison Square Garden in eight years. COVID restrictions be damned, the powers that be drastically relaxed restrictions on public gatherings right before the playoffs. As such, after only allowing 2,000 fans per game in the regular season, over 15,000 (including yours truly) packed MSG for Game 1. That electric atmosphere was the awakening of a sleeping giant, not to be undone by the forced masks, vaccine cards, and all the drama that happened in the world. For a while, it looked like they’d all get to celebrate. The Knicks woke up from a truly awful first quarter to hold the lead for much of the fourth quarter. With a minute to go, they led 103-100 and seemed to force a turnover on the baseline, but the ball bounced off the chest of RJ Barrett and somehow landed right in the lap of Bogdan Bogdanovic, who nailed a game-tying three. That shot honestly haunts me more than what comes next, because if it didn’t happen, he never gets the chance. I really don’t know why, but the F— Trae Young chants were prevalent well before the final seconds where he would immortalize himself. Maybe we couldn’t help ourselves from giving life to a new New York villain after years in the darkness. Tied at 105 in the final 10 seconds, Thibodeau inserted an ice-cold Frank Ntilikina into the game to defend Young. As the team’s best defender, it made sense in a vacuum, but it clearly didn’t go well. Young cooked Ntilikina and drew Gibson out of the paint for an ill-advised double team. There was no containment on the right side, allowing the floater maestro to get downhill and put up an easy go-ahead floater with 0.9 seconds to go to cap a 32-point night for the win. His villainous persona would only grow over the coming days and weeks. Knicks fans got their cathartic playoff win two nights later, but midnight struck on this Cinderella run in a hurry, as they lost in five games. It turns out that injury to Robinson was crucial, as Clint Capela bullied the Knicks’ backup bigs into submission. There are all sorts of humiliating moments in this series. Reggie Bullock’s infamous tweet, the pumpkin that All-NBA and MVP candidate Julius Randle turned into, and Trae’s bow to end the series at the Garden. It wasn’t the way anyone wanted it to end, but there was hope for the first time in a long time. But as is customary with the Knicks, hope is immediately met with hardship, as we saw in the following season. When a team overachieves with a young roster, the front office is given a few different decisions. They can either ignore the season that happened and continue to stay the course, even if it means a backslide, or accelerate the rebuild. Leon Rose chose the second option, going all-in on surrounding a nucleus of Randle, Robinson, and RJ Barrett with veteran talent. They re-signed Alec Burks, Derrick Rose, and Nerlens Noel. They gave Evan Fournier $72 million in free agency. They even brought home hometown hero Kemba Walker after he was bought out by OKC to stabilize the point guard position. There were few teams with better vibes when the 2021-22 season began than the Knicks, especially after they beat the Celtics to open the season. Just look at the Sidetalk crowd! A 5-1 start had everyone dreaming of a steady ascent, but this season got bad fast. The Knicks hoped that Thibodeau’s scheme, coupled with the hard-nosed defensive identity from the season prior, could at least balance out the bad defenders added to the roster. That was a hard no, as the team fell to 11th in defensive rating. The team also got a hard regression from Randle, injuries to Derrick Rose and Nerlens Noel, and the drama with the repeated benching of Walker after it was clear he was well past effectiveness. The vibes turned sour fast, as we’ll get into. By the end of the season, they spiraled to 37-45, missing the play-in tournament altogether. It was a weirdly strong East that year, and the Knicks fell so far behind. On January 6, 2022, the Knicks were sitting at just 18-20. There was still time to preserve the season, but with how rancid the vibes were getting, they needed a spark and fast. They thought they’d get that with Barrett’s improbable game-winner over Jayson Tatum that night, but that was not the thing that was talked about in the media the next day. In the midst of a miserable down season where he looked a lot more like the player who vanished in the playoffs than the All-NBA stud he was in the regular season, Randle had enough of the boos from a hostile Garden crowd and started booing them back. What was with New York athletes booing the fans in 2021??? This only torpedoed the vibes from that season even more, turning a man who briefly became one of New York’s most beloved athletes into one that fans would never fully get behind again. A rocky offseason would follow, where a large portion of fans and media called on Leon Rose to trade him to pave the way for Obi Toppin to get a real opportunity he was denied by Randle’s breakout in 2021. Randle would stay and even become an All-Star again, but fans’ resentment continued. Throughout his next few years as a Knick, even as he rebounded as a player, he would be blamed for their failure. It would last until he was traded to Minnesota in September 2024, with his PR as a Knick never quite rebounding from that day in January 2022. What was honestly the worst part of that entire season was the fact that the team embarrassed themselves on a nightly basis, blowing historic levels of big leads as part of a complete collapse. After the team got to 22-21 in mid-January, they lost 17 of their next 21 games in embarrassing fashion. January 18 vs. MIN: Knicks lead in the final four minutes, but fall behind after an and-one by Karl-Anthony Towns. Randle misses a free throw with 24 seconds that would’ve tied it. Down two at the buzzer, Burks misses a three. February 5 @ LAL: Knicks lead by 21 in the first half, but after going up 68-47, they concede a 33-11 run in eight minutes. A miraculous rally from Barrett got them to overtime, but the Knicks go 2-for-11 with two turnovers in the next five minutes to lose. February 14 vs. OKC: Knicks lead by four in the final minute, but commit a pair of fouls that allow OKC to tie it. Quentin Grimes hits a go-ahead layup with 15 seconds left, but Darius Bazley matches it with a game-tying layup with five seconds to go. Randle missed a shot at the buzzer, and the Knicks got dominated in OT, but they had a chance with a game-tying three-point attempt by Immanuel Quickley at the death… which missed. February 16 @ BKN: Against an injured Nets team that was starting Patty Mills, Seth Curry, and James Johnson, the Knicks built a 28-point lead in the second quarter and led by as much as 19 in the fourth. They blew that lead, as Cam Thomas exploded for 16 off the bench to stun the Knicks on a game-ending 38-15 run. After the biggest choke in franchise history, the Knicks went into the All-Star break an extremely demoralized 25-34. March 4 @ PHX: Randle loses his temper in the third quarter with a 10-point lead late in the third and gets ejected. The Suns go on a ferocious comeback against an undermanned Knicks team, rallying from 14 down in the fourth to stun them at the buzzer with a Cam Johnson buzzer-beater. This would be the low water mark of the season, as the Knicks began a strong 12-7 finish to the season two nights later against the Clippers. They would get one more embarrassment after the season was already done for when they blew a 23-point lead to a healthy Nets team in April, being outscored 60-31 in the second half. In all, the Knicks blew 19 fourth-quarter leads and 15 double-digit leads in 2021-22. They blew four 20-point leads. In the four years since, they’ve blown two total (November 2022 vs. ATL, April 2024 vs. CLE). We didn’t know it at the time, but signing Jalen Brunson in the summer of 2022 would be unimaginably franchise-changing for the Knicks. What is sometimes hard to remember is that it didn’t start well. The Knicks were once again downtrodden to start the 2022-23 season. They’d trade big wins with ridiculous losses, and would usually save the most embarrassing stretches for Sunday matinees at MSG. Three weeks before this game against Dallas, the Knicks scored 48 in the first quarter and still lost to OKC after allowing a ridiculous 145 points. On December 3, 2022, the Knicks once again jumped out to a big lead at home against a Western Conference foe, using a late burst to go up 32-20 after one. That lead expanded to 15 early in the second quarter, leading 38-23. Then… they didn’t score another point for five minutes. The Mavericks came back to tie it, but the Knicks snapped out of it to go up 59-52 at halftime. What could go wrong? Well, that Mavericks team was pretty dangerous with Luka Doncic. Over the next 17 minutes, they blitzed the Knicks to an unbelievable degree to take a 30-point lead. In less than 17 minutes of game action, they outscored the hapless ‘Bockers 61-24, turning what was a fine Sunday afternoon in the Garden to a loud, hostile environment for the home team. When the final buzzer sounded, the Knicks had fallen to 10-13, a continuation of the previous season’s drama. At this point, with the memories of that magical 2020-21 season seeming further and further away, the team reached an inflection point. Under previous executives or with a more hands-on James Dolan, this would’ve been the time for a big trade or a firing to shake things up. Hell, the Knicks were extremely close to firing Thibodeau during this time as his seat got hotter and hotter. Would the Knicks make the same mistake that they had made in the previous 20 years to throw them back into incompetence? Leon was not quite willing to go there yet. The Knicks won the next day against the Cavaliers and wound up winning eight in a row after benching Evan Fournier, D-Rose, and Cam Reddish. By allowing Thibodeau to rein in his culture instead of ditching him like previous regimes would do, Leon might’ve saved this era of Knicks basketball before it even began. After starting 10-13, the Knicks exploded into becoming what they were destined to be. With an extremely deep bench of young talent surrounding veteran All-Stars Randle and Brunson, the Knicks soared to a 47-35 record and a No. 5 seed in the East, permanently washing away the bad vibes of last season. They cleared the first barrier to contention by dominating the Cavaliers in five games in the first round, and got a stroke of luck when the powerhouse Milwaukee Bucks lost in the first round to the No. 8 seed, but while the Knicks would get home-court advantage in the second round for the first time in a generation, they’d be doing it against Jimmy Butler and Erik Spolestra. As such, it didn’t go well as experience met youth. The Knicks fell behind 3-1 before a heroic 48-minute performance from Brunson extended the season in Game 5, forcing a pivotal in Game 6 in South Beach. As he continued to bud into a superstar, Brunson was on fire that night, carrying the Knicks offense. Quickley was hurt, Barrett was struggling, and Randle was both. The one time they sat Brunson, they conceded an 8-0 run in 1:53 that took away an early seven-point lead and momentum that they would never quite regain. Still, as the game grew tighter and tighter down the stretch, the Knicks had a chance to force a Game 7 at MSG. 26 years after the Knicks blew a 3-1 lead to the Heat, they had a chance to rectify a decades-old injustice. A four-point sequence in the final minute after a flagrant foul cut the deficit to two. After the Knicks got the stop, they had the ball with 30 seconds left. Brunson had 39 points, the rest of the team had 51. He was the only choice to take the shot. He drove on Butler into the help, ultimately trapping him in a double team. With his teammates clearing out the right side, he was all alone. Instead of taking the shot or kicking it out to Josh Hart behind him, he tried to shovel the ball to a cutting Randle. The ghosts from 1997 were just too strong to overcome. The Heat would hit two free throws on the other end, Grimes would airball a three, and that was that. The best season in two decades ended in a whimper. A subplot around that time caused a lot of controversy, and it dates back to the Kristaps Porzingis trade. The Knicks received two first-round picks in that massive January 2019 trade, one of which was unprotected in 2021 and become Grimes, and the other was top-10 protected in 2023. With how promising the young duo of Doncic and Porzingis was, nobody thought the 2023 pick would be close to not conveying. That was until the 2022-23 season completely fell apart for the Mavericks. Injuries to key role players, a lack of gelling between Luka and Kyrie, and a myriad of other factors had the Mavs on the cusp of missing the play-in tournament. Dallas lost nine of their last 11 games, including a shameless mid-April tank job that saw them pull Luka after just 11 minutes in Game 81 in a loss to the Bulls. It not only ensured they’d miss the play-in, but also ensured that they would jump to 10th in the lottery odds. As long as Adam Silver didn’t screw them, they’d get to keep their pick. Which is exactly what happened. The Knicks would have their pick deferred to 2024, where it would fall to No. 25 because the man that the Mavs picked in the lottery, Dereck Lively II, helped stabilize their frontcourt en route to an NBA Finals appearance. Funny how that works. Back to things the Knicks can actually control, they were once again teetering on the edge to start the 2023-24 season. Sitting at just 17-14 on December 30, 2023, they made a bold move, dealing Barrett and Quickley for OG Anunoby in the first of three all-in trades that would complete the infinity gauntlet of a roster they would eventually possess. For that one month in January 2024, the Knicks were unstoppable. The lineup of Brunson, Donte DiVincenzo, Anunoby, Randle, and Isaiah Hartenstein was historically good. They produced one of the best months in franchise history, going 16-2 and going from a team that would struggle to stay out of the play-in to a team that could rise up to the juggernaut Celtics and go toe-to-toe with them On January 27, the Knicks were rolling to their sixth consecutive win, up double digits late against the very Heat team that knocked them out a year prior. With 4:3o to go and the starters still in, Randle drove to the basket. Jaime Jaquez Jr. attempted to draw a charge, undercutting the rising 6’8” forward and leaving him vulnerable in midair. By the time he came down, he had dislocated his shoulder. Nobody knew it at the time, but it would be the last time Randle wore the orange and blue. He would attempt to return for the playoffs, but shut it down after a setback in April. He would fully heal, but would be traded to Minnesota ahead of training camp that September. This would be just one of the several mind-numbing injuries that would derail the 2024 Knicks. Despite missing Randle and even Anunoby for stretches, the Knicks won 50 games and took the No. 2 seed in the East, thanks to heroic work from Brunson. In classic Knicks fashion, they were rewarded by playing the criminally underseeded Sixers, who stumbled into the play-in due to injuries and were considered one of the best teams in the East. Go figure. That first-round series was an instant classic. Every game was a war. Josh Hart’s Game 1 dagger, the miracle at the end of Game 2, Precious Achiuwa’s grit in Game 4, all of it was awesome. It looked like this war of attrition was won by the Knicks in five games. Deuce McBride splashed a mid-range jumper to go up six with 29 seconds left. MSG was in celebration mode. Then, Tyrese Maxey pulled them back from the depths. He baited Robinson into jumping on a three-point attempt, burying it to eventually complete a four-point play. After Hart was fouled with 15 seconds left, he split bot free throws, keeping it a one-possession game. At this point, you can see Thibodeau yelling for a foul from the sideline. The Sixers know that’s likely the plan, so with no timeouts, they go quickly up the floor. Embiid does a give-and-go at halfcourt with Maxey, who decides to fire from 35 feet… and bury it. With two timeouts, the Knicks decide to just play it out with eight seconds left, ultimately generating a rushed floater from Brunson that was blocked by Nic Batum. Overtime. In overtime, the Knicks led for much of the first two minutes, but things changed when a fastbreak layup for Hart didn’t go down, and Maxey hit Kelly Oubre Jr. on an outlet for a go-ahead layup. The offense short-circuited, but Brunson bailed them out with a game-tying three with one minute to go. The Sixers went ahead on an Oubre layup, but the Knicks had the ball with a chance to tie or take the lead with 25 seconds left. Brunson sized up Batum and fired… into the crowd. At the last second, he decided to pass instead of shoot, and threw it away as Hartenstein cut for the basket. For the second year in a row, a playoff loss would end with indecision from the captain. The Knicks would wind up picking themselves up off the mat to win Game 6 and close out the series, but it reinforced something that remains an issue even after the title. In the last 25 years, the Knicks have only closed out one playoff series at home, in 2025 against Boston. That’s it. That 2024 team was a dead man walking. The injuries continued to pile up, but even then, they led 2-0 on the Pacers in the second round. They were two wins away from a date with the Celtics, where sure, they were likely to be pummeled, but it would be progress for a downtrodden organization. The Knicks led Game 3 by nine in the fourth. It’s sometimes hard to forget that it looked like a 3-0 lead was happening for a lot of that game, but it did. The Pacers did what they always did, riding incredible offense back into the game over and over again. It was tied with six minutes left. The next six minutes would be a grudge match. The two teams would trade clutch buckets, stops, and physicality. The Pacers pulled ahead by three late, only for Brunson to drive a stake into their hearts with 41 seconds left to tie it. (Side note: 2024 Brunson was the best player I’ve ever watched. Period). Indiana got the ball on the next possession, but it was 23 seconds of defensive brilliance from the Knicks. The Pacers were rigid, motionless, and indecisive. For maybe the only time in those two series did they look afraid offensively. Some great rotations forced the ball out of Tyrese Haliburton’s hands late in the shot clock and into Andrew Nembhard’s. Nembhard touched the ball with four on the clock and 35 feet from the basket. He took a few dribbles, then stepped back. He was five feet behind the three-point line and heaving out of desperation after being handed a grenade. In all of NBA history, this shot almost never goes in. In another life, that shot doesn’t go in, and the Knicks win Game 3 and the series. They grow up a lot sooner. Maybe they don’t make the trade for KAT, seeing DiVincenzo as too crucial and Randle as the missing piece to get over the top. While heartbreaking to remember, maybe it was for the best. The Pacers were the better team in 2025. Anyone who says otherwise is lying. Now 2024? They absolutely weren’t. That was a seven-game series that the Pacers won because the entire Knicks roster fell apart. In case you forgot, let’s do a roll call of the injuries, shall we? Julius Randle: dislocates shoulder in late January, out for the season. Mitchell Robinson: Already on the mend from ankle injuries earlier in the season, he was pulled down by Joel Embiid while rising for a layup in Game 3 vs. Philly, landing awkwardly on the ankle with a stress fracture. He would miss Game 4, return for the next few games, and ultimately undergo surgery after Game 1 against Indiana due to that same ankle. He wouldn’t play again until February 2025. Bojan Bogdanovic: Had the ball at the top of the key early in Game 4, when it was stripped by Batum. While pursuing the ball, Batum fell and landed on the 35-year-old’s left ankle with his full body weight. He would miss the remainder of the postseason with a foot/ankle injury and would wind up suffering setback after setback. The injury would ultimately end his career. OG Anunoby: After months of being heavily relied on, the oft-injured Anunoby suffered a left hamstring strain while on a fast break in Game 2 against Indiana. He would try his hardest to return, ultimately playing five minutes in Game 7 with a severe hamstring issue before shutting it down. Josh Hart: While he never missed time, the Knicks’ glue guy was suffering from serious abdominal soreness in Game 6, to the point where he was a game-time decision in Game 7. Isaiah Hartenstein: In a similar vein, Hartenstein suffered a left shoulder pinched-nerve issue in Game 4 against Indiana. He never missed time, but played significantly worse that series than he had all season. Jalen Brunson: As the icing on the cake, a man who would routinely turn his ankle and cause scares across the Tri-State Area, would wind up suffering a completely different injury. While Game 7 continued to get further and further away from the Knicks, Brunson fractured his hand on Haliburton’s kneecap in the third quarter, ending his season. This mountain of issues was too much to overcome and would officially mark the end of this core after a historically awful defensive showing in Game 7. The all-in push that would come would bring the Knicks to glory. but not without countless drama and failure. Those all-in moves brought in Mikal Bridges and Karl-Anthony Towns at the expense of fan favorites and a plethora of draft picks. It was the completion of the master plan. While there were more moves on the margins to be made, this was the core that they pushed all the chips in for. They had no choice. The big thing with this team was that they were built to beat the reigning champions. They had assembled a pair of elite defensive wings to match Jayson Tatum and Jaylen Brown, a plethora of shooters up and down the roster to beat them, and a stretch-five who could drag out their rim protectors. That matchup with Boston would be emphasized all year. Well, the schedule makers sent the new-look Knicks for a trial by fire in Boston on their Ring Night. There would be no championship hangover (yet) for the C’s that night, as they took it right to the Knicks all night long. They looked like a team that had never played together against a fully healthy juggernaut on the other side. It was an embarrassment on national television. They allowed 43 points in the first quarter, they were down 22 just 15 minutes into the game, and they would trail by as much as 35 in a game that was never competitive. On that note, the Knicks were never competitive against Boston all season long. The two met again in February, and this time there was no excuse for inexperience, with a 27-point beatdown. Two weeks later, it happened again. The fourth meeting would be the most competitive, but the Knicks blew a late lead in regulation before faltering in overtime. 0-4 and outscored by 64 points. Yet, it didn’t wind up mattering. They got smoked again in the first halves of Game 1 and Game 2 of that second-round playoff series and they learned the lessons from a terrible regular season to come back in both. Their resilience was unbelievable, but eventually, they’d encounter something they can’t overcome. One of the big ghosts that have haunted the Knicks for generations is the inability to get past the Pacers. While the 90s rivalry was more 50/50 than the media would like you to believe, the pain from Reggie Miller to the Ewing finger roll to Roy Hibbert’s block to the entire team falling apart in 2024 hurt. Game 1 of the Eastern Conference Finals. It’s the first time in 25 years that the Knicks are at this stage. A quarter of a century. They have home-court advantage too. This had to be the year. For a lot of Game 1, it looked like it was going to be. They led by 15 after a Mikal jumper with 4:55 to go. They led by 14 after a Brunson three with 2:51 to go. They led by 8 after a KAT layup with 41 seconds to go. Aaron Nesmith, silent all game long, started to catch fire. He made one three after another three after another three. The Knicks melted down. They missed free throws, they turned it over, and they completely broke down defensively. It seemed so ridiculous to watch in real time. You shrugged it off at first, for getting just how rough the history of the franchise was, but slowly, your eyes start to widen in horror. Leading by one with seven seconds left, Anunoby went to the line. He missed one of the two free throws, meaning the Knicks only led by two. With no timeouts, Haliburton ran up the floor, charged into the paint, and ran back out to the three-point line. As if the basketball gods were intentionally trying to play another sick joke, Haliburton seemed to move like he was being controlled by a joystick, to then fire a shot at the buzzer that would clank off the back of the rim and somehow drop perfectly through the net. He could retry that shot 1,000,000 times and would never do that again. The most insane, improbable thing ever on a basketball court just forced overtime, but the Knicks were already mentally defeated. Even funnier was the fact that the Knicks dragged you back in to start overtime to take an early lead to make you believe again. The Knicks led by four with just under three minutes to go in OT. They forced a turnover and ran up the court. Brunson received the ball under the basket and laid it up off the glass… only for it to be blocked by Myles Turner in an obvious goaltend that was uncalled. The immediate momentum of the play swung back for a Nembhard three. That five-point swing decided the game. By the time the final whistle blew, the Knicks were dead. They’d have a huge 20-point comeback in Game 3 and have an inspiring Game 5 win, but they were dead. Year 52 had come and gone. The drought continues. It would cost Tom Thibodeau his job, but ultimately usher in the final piece of the puzzle. Hiring Mike Brown would prove to be an awesome decision for Leon Rose and company, but the process to get there was a PR nightmare. Firing Thibodeau created a media storm by itself in the sense that many believed that the Knicks were scapegoating him for bad roster construction and were ungrateful for the man who helped restore them to relevancy, but the month-long process that it took to find a replacement made it worse. Now, nothing the Knicks did was actually bad. They were the only vacancy when they fired Thibs, which allowed them to do what they wanted, but it was the way it was reported. They called about a bunch of currently established coaches before being obviously rejected. Looking back, it reminds me of how Penn State football conducted their recent coaching search. Odd stuff. The rumors about convincing Jay Wright to come back to the Jason Kidd saga to the constant clowning on social media all culminated in the hiring of Brown, who would unlock the Knicks in a way that nobody thought he could. The Knicks never reached that next gear, but they won 53 games in a solid campaign that included an NBA Cup title. Immediately following that NBA Cup title, though, the Knicks fell apart as a team, both injury-wise and play-wise. Sitting at 23-9 on New Year’s Eve, the Knicks led by 17 early on the road against the Spurs and by double digits when Victor Wembanyama left due to injury in the fourth. They still blew it, thanks to an all-time heater from Julian Champagnie. That sparked an unbelievably awful 2-9 stretch, one that would lead to a ridiciulous amount of discourse at the worst time of year. As part of his 2-9 skid, the Knicks battled injuries to Hart and Landry Shamet while they got smoked by the Hawks and Sixers. A monthly embarrassment at the hands of the Pistons followed, as did a late struggle against the Suns in Phoenix. There was the Brunson injury in Sacramento and the subsequent 17-point blown first-quarter lead to the Warriors in San Francisco. When the Knicks returned home from the West Coast, they were greeted by boos in another loss to the Suns. Two days later, in a Monday matinee on MLK Day against the Mavericks, rock bottom. The Knicks had their largest halftime deficit in 11 years. They were thrown around, humiliated, and utterly embarrassed by a severely shorthanded and terrible Mavericks team in an eerily similar manner to the inflection point that happened in December 2022. After this game, the discourse was toxic. The hostility toward Mike Brown, Mikal Bridges, and Karl-Anthony Towns was at an all-time high. There were real talks about disassembling the core before they would even complete their second season. With pressure mounting on Leon Rose and the entire organization, they decided not to do anything drastic before the trade deadline. Once again, patience was rewarded. If you haven’t already, I recommend watching the new hour-long documentary on the championship run produced by MSG. I’ll link it here. Anyway, they provided such a great perspective about the opportunity that the Knicks had going into this postseason, and one they knew they were blowing through Game 3 of the Hawks series. They were coasting with a double-digit lead in the fourth quarter of Game 2, but Jose Alvarado poked the bear in CJ McCollum, who embraced his inner Trae to score 32 points in a miraculous comeback effort for the Hawks, one that ended in a missed game-winner by Bridges at the buzzer that only increased the scrutiny on him. Three nights later in Atlanta, the Hawks led by as much as 18 in a blitz of a first half, but the Knicks rallied all the way back to take the lead late. Once again, we hit another brutal break in a playoff game against Atlanta, just like Game 1 in 2021. The Knicks led 108-105 in the final minute when Jalen Johnson drove to the cup. Towns, who would have his incredible breakthrough two days after this, blocked him at the rim, but the ball ricocheted off the bottom of the backboard and into his lap for a layup. Instead of having the ball with a three-point lead and 50 seconds left, it was a one-point game. Fast forward to a tie game in the final 20 seconds. McCollum gets the inbound, sizes up the formidable McBride, and buries a mid-range jumper in his face. On the other end, Brunson would isolate, as he always does. He would dribble, drive, stop, pump… and throw it away. Just like Game 6 against Miami in 2023 and Game 5 against Philly in 2024. The ghosts of the past struck again and handed the Knicks another unbelievably awful playoff heartbreak. They were now two losses away from a humiliating first-round exit and an offseason that would likely see massive changes. They had to figure it out here. They had no choice anymore. They responded. They’d win the final three games of the Atlanta series by a total of 96 points- historic dominance. They’d completely bulldoze the Sixers in a sweep, destroying them to smithereens in Games 1 and 4 to humiliate them so much they’d have to beg and plead for a 41-year-old who was dreaming of the Big Apple to come save them. Once again, it was Game 1 of the ECF. At home. This time against a Cavs team they decimated three years ago. It was a sluggish first half, mainly charged by the Knicks’ rusty shooting, but they still had a double-digit lead in the second quarter. That fell apart in a hurry. After the Knicks took a 38-27 lead, the Cavs went on a prolonged 66-33 run to take a 22-point lead with 7:50 to go. It was happening again. One year after the Haliburton embarrassment, the Knicks were being run out of the gym just when they seemed to be making progress. The ghosts were burying them even more than the bricks from their ice-cold shooting. Honestly, it’s a shame what happened next would be mostly forgotten because of Game 4 of the Finals. This was the significantly harder comeback, it was just in a much lower leverage game. At this point, it was hard to really do anything to shake this Knicks team. They had made the NBA Finals for the first time in 27 years, they had won a pair of road games in said Finals, they had overcome a million improbable deficits over the last few years. What more could they overcome? Well, how about an unpopular president murdering the vibes of the first Finals home game of the 21st century and the Spurs completely blitzing the Knicks to start Game 4, taking a near-30-point lead in the second half on the backs of hot shooting. Barring a ridiculous collapse, the Spurs were going to even up the series and head back to San Antonio needing to just defend home court twice to win the Finals. The Knicks had spoiled an unbelievable opportunity in winning the first two on the road, only to give home court right back. It was the last gasps of those ghosts, who had almost completely been defeated to this point. The only ones that seemed to be left were the ones from 1994 and 1999, from when the Knicks finished one Hakeem finger-tip away from a title in the former and fell to these very Spurs in the latter. The agony of coming so close had haunted the Ewings and Starks of the world for 30 years, as did many fans. But at this point? The only choice that this team had to was to overcome the odds once again. This will be the second consecutive part that goes over 7,000 words. I’ve written over 20,000 about this 53-year drought over the last month and change. Tonight is going to be something special, something that we will never forget. At times, it doesn’t quite sink in that the Knicks really did it, but it will tonight. It’s a team that I’ve loved my whole life, but said life has been much shorter than a lot of people I’m surrounded by, whether it’s in the P&T community, my friends, my family, there’s always someone who’s suffered more. I’ve shared this story before, but I truly will never forget where I was, what I was doing, and who I was with when the buzzer sounded in Game 5. Watching poolside in the backyard, I immediately hugged my 39-year-old brother who had lived through so much more pain and suffering watching this team than I have. It was emotional, and an experience that I know a lot of you shared with your loved ones. That’s what sports fandom can do. It can cause agony and dread to a degree that’s not healthy for, let’s be honest, things we can’t control and people who don’t know who we are. But it can also cause great moments, one that we all got on June 13 and will get again tonight. This organization has come a long way in 53 years. They’ve cycled through foundational pieces, coaches, executives, ownership, and controversy after controversy. What we got in Leon Rose, the architect of this team, in 2020 is something that this franchise should be eternally grateful for. After decades of absolute buffoons in the front office, there was a calculated maestro who placed value in every small detail and exercised patience when necessary, while also being able to make big moves when the time is right. Only one of the players that Rose inherited saw the fruits of this rebuild. The coach that he hired to change that culture also watched from afar. His original plan fizzled out, but the thing about great executives is that they find a way to figure it out, taking what the universe gives him. This era brought about a new type of pain. The pain that only those ghosts from the 90s felt. The pain of knowing you have something special, only for it to be repeatedly ripped away and beaten down. The group that Leon wound up building, though, had the perseverance that nobody in this franchise had in the last 53 seasons. Such perseverance allowed them to take everything that happened in the six-year agonizing climb to the top in stride, using it as fuel to ultimately create an unstoppable force that nobody could deny, not even the mountain of ghosts that acted as a brick wall for generations of players in the orange and blue. We’ve been told a trade is needed to keep both, but what if I told you that’s not quite the case? Knickstape gave fans the best basketball they’ve seen in a decade, then one man plunged them into a second dark age. With two games down and three to go before the Knicks open their regular season, here’s who’s who in the preseason. Into the 21st century, we encounter the bleakest decade in Knicks history. title: The Supreme Court’s next major case on the free exercise of religion - SCOTUSblog
content: On Nov. 3, the Supreme Court will hear argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy. This case raises important questions about how far the court will go in expanding the Constitution’s protections of the free exercise of religion. One of the most dramatic changes in constitutional law in recent years has concerned the religion clauses of the First Amendment. For decades, the Supreme Court took a robust approach to the establishment clause, seeing it as best described by Thomas Jefferson’s metaphor of a wall separating church and state. At the same time, the court took a much weaker approach to the free exercise clause, as embodied in its decision in Employment Division v. Smith, which held that the First Amendment does not provide a basis for religious exemptions from general laws. But, in recent years, the court has completely reversed this. It has greatly lessened the protections of the establishment clause; a majority of the current justices reject the idea of a wall separating church and state. In its most recent case about that provision, 2022’s Kennedy v. Bremerton School District, the court declared: “‘[T]he line’ that courts and governments ‘must draw between the permissible and the impermissible’ has to ‘accor[d] with history and faithfully reflec[t] the understanding of the Founding Fathers.’” Given this, it is likely that only government coercion to worship or adhere to a particular religion will be found to violate the establishment clause. By contrast, the Supreme Court has aggressively expanded the protections of the free exercise clause. In 2021’s Fulton v. City of Philadelphia, the court held that it violates the free exercise of religion for the city, in contracting with private entities to place children in foster care, to insist that contractors not discriminate based on sexual orientation when they had a religious reason for doing so. In 2022’s Carson v. Makin, as well as 2018’s Trinity Lutheran v. Comer and 2020’s Espinoza v. Montana Department of Revenue, the court ruled that it violates the free exercise of religion for the state to provide aid to private secular schools that it denies to religious schools. And in 2025’s Mahmoud v. Taylor, the court held that it violates the free exercise of religion for a school system to fail to give parents of elementary school students notice and a chance to opt their children out of a curriculum that presented “LGBTQ+- inclusive” storybooks. Colorado’s universal preschool program funds preschools – public, private, and religious alike – that sign an agreement to give children an “equal opportunity to enroll” regardless of, among other things, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, or gender identity. Two Catholic parish preschools and the Archdiocese of Denver say that they have a religious belief that they must consider a family’s sexual orientation and gender identity in admissions, and they sued under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 for an injunction against the preschool requirement. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10 Circuit upheld the Colorado law, applying Employment Division v. Smith and explaining that the Colorado law is a neutral law of general applicability; it was not motivated by a desire to apply to religion and applies equally to all. The court also explained that Colorado was not denying funding to religious schools that it provides to secular institutions: No preschool taking state money can refuse to admit children because of the race, religion, sexual orientation, or gender identity of the parents. The Supreme Court granted certiorari on two questions: (1) Whether proving a lack of general applicability under Smith requires showing unfettered discretion or categorical exemptions for identical secular conduct; and (2) whether Carson v. Makin (that the government violates the free exercise clause if it denies funds to religious schools that it provides to private secular schools) displaces the rule of Smith only when the government explicitly excludes religious people and institutions. There are many underlying issues that could make the case enormously important. First, will the court overrule Employment Division v. Smith and, if so, what will replace it? The court did not grant review on this question, but it certainly underlies the case. Five years ago, in Fulton v. City of Philadelphia, Justice Samuel Alito wrote a lengthy opinion concurring in the judgment, joined by Justices Clarence Thomas and Neil Gorsuch, urging the overruling of Smith. Justice Amy Coney Barrett wrote a concurring opinion, joined in full by Justice Brett Kavanaugh, in which she said that she agreed with much of Alito’s opinion, but that overruling Smith would raise many difficult questions and there was no need for the court to resolve them in the case before it. Petitioner St. Mary Catholic Parish clearly is urging the court to jettison Smith. The first argument in its brief is that the “Court rarely applies Smith.” It says: “Out of the eighteen free exercise cases this Court has resolved since Smith in 1990, this Court has relied on Smith only twice to rule against the religious objector,” and one of these was Smith itself. But the brief says that lower courts, like the 10th in this case, constantly rely on Smith. The ideological shift on the court with regard to free exercise claims has been dramatic. The majority opinion in Smith was written by Justice Antonin Scalia and it was liberals at the time that were critical of this holding. Now, it is the most conservative justices who are urging Smith’s overruling and it is the liberal justices who are defending it. Smith was about whether Native Americans should have a constitutional right to a religious exemption from a law prohibiting consumption of peyote – a hallucinogenic substance. Now, the cases are about Christians, such as the Catholic Church in St. Mary Catholic Parish, that are seeking religious exemptions. Second, there is the question of when religion is infringed. If the court overrules Smith, this issue will become much more salient, as will the court’s need to define what is “religion” and a “religious belief.” Under Smith, with no exemptions for any religion, there is far less need to face these questions. For instance, in St. Mary Catholic Parish, there is a question of whether the Colorado law infringes the church’s religious beliefs. The Colorado statute does not limit the ability of the Catholic schools to teach whatever they choose. The law simply says that a school receiving government funds should not discriminate against children, including based on the sexual orientation or the gender identity of the parents. The Catholic Church certainly may say that its teachings condemn same-sex sexual activity and gender transitions. But their contention in the present case is that their religion requires that they discriminate against children because of their parents being gay, lesbian, or transgender. This seems a much more difficult argument unless the court is going to accord considerable deference to religious claims in applying the free exercise clause. Third, even if the court overrules Smith, does the government have a compelling interest in preventing discrimination against children on account of the sexual orientation or gender identity of their parents? In 2018’s Masterpiece Cakeshop v. Colorado Civil Rights Commission, the court considered the question of whether a baker had a right under the free exercise clause to violate a Colorado civil rights statute by refusing to design and bake a wedding cake for a gay couple. The court ruled narrowly, holding that members of the Colorado Civil Rights Commission had expressed impermissible animus towards religion. In 2023’s 303 Creative v. Elenis, the court held that it would violate the freedom of speech to apply a civil rights statute to force a website designer to provide her wedding services for same-sex couples. The court did not consider her claim based on the free exercise of religion. There always is a tension between liberty and equality. Any law that prohibits discrimination limits the freedom to discriminate. For decades, the Supreme Court was clear that prohibiting discrimination was more important than protecting the right to discriminate. In 1968’s Newman v. Piggy Park Enterprises, Inc., the court summarily rejected a claim that a person’s religious beliefs were a basis to discriminate in violation of civil rights statutes. If the court overrules Smith, or says that strict scrutiny should be used under Smith, the question will need to be addressed: should the free exercise of religion provide a right to harm others by discriminating against them? Fourth, if the government provides funding for schools, may it deny funding to schools that discriminate based on their religious beliefs? In a series of cases culminating most recently in Carson v. Makin, the court has held that the government violates the free exercise clause if it denies funds to religious schools that it provides to private secular schools. St. Mary Catholic Parish argues that Colorado is doing just that: denying it funding because of its exercising its religious beliefs and excluding children whose parents are gay, lesbian, or transgender. But Colorado argues that its law does not discriminate based on religion. It will pay for children to attend preschools that are religious so long as they do not discriminate against children based on their parents’ sexual orientation or gender identity. In Carson, the Maine statute paid for children in areas without public schools to attend private schools but denied funding for children attending religious schools. Colorado says that its law is different because it does not exclude such institutions. The Supreme Court could rule in favor of Colorado by applying Employment Division v. Smith. But the conservative majority – and especially Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch, Kavanaugh, and Barrett – want to expand the protections of the free exercise of religion. St. Mary’s Catholic Parish v. Roy could provide them the opportunity to do so and thereby dramatically change the law. Erwin Chemerinsky is the Dean and Jesse H. Choper Distinguished Professor of Law, University of California, Berkeley School of Law. title: Rev. Mark V Garringer Obituary - The Star Press
content: Rev. Mark V Garringer, age 86, Farmland, died Friday October 16, 2026 at home following an extended illness.  Born in Winchester on March 25, 1940, he grew up in the Farmland area and was a part of the last graduating class of Green Township High School – the class of 1958.  Mark furthered his education at Taylor University where he received a B.A. in Bible Literacy.  As a Congregational Christian Pastor, Mark served in ministry for nearly 60 years, pastoring in Randolph and Delaware Counties.  Along with his wife, he served with OMS International for a year in Haiti and at the Greenwood (IN) mission headquarters as Assistant Director of Field Ministries in the mid 1980s.  During his final years of pastoring near Selma, Mark served as Men’s Evening Supervisor at the Muncie Mission; his work there was a ministry he cherished.  As a carpenter, he played an integral role in designing, planning, and building a house in Muncie to sell to support OMS.  He also designed and built four duplexes for seniors in Albany.  Mark had a heart of compassion and while he enjoyed farming and mushroom hunting, his biggest joy was in taking care of people. Survivors include his wife of 65 years, Linda Sue “Susie” (Swingley) Garringer; daughter: Gina Garringer, Farmland; son: Jordan Garringer (wife: Lacie), Albany; brother: Lee Garringer (wife: Joyce), Muncie; grandson: Taylor Garringer, and granddaughter: Audrey Garringer. He is preceded in death by his son, Ralph Aaron Garringer; parents: Verlin & Nellie (Lasley) Garringer; brother: Roy Garringer; and nephews: David Garringer, Sr. and James Lee Garringer. Visitation will be Wednesday October 21, 2026 from 3 until 6 p.m. at Meacham Funeral Service with the funeral ceremony at 6 p.m.  Burial will take place on Thursday at Hopewell Cemetery with graveside services at 3 p.m. Preferred memorials are to the Muncie Mission or The Gideons International; condolences and other expressions of sympathy may be given at www.MeachamFuneralService.com. title: PREVIEW | Paris Saint-Germain v FC Barcelona - FC Barcelona
content: FC Barcelona's impeccable start to 2026/27 continued on Saturday with perhaps the toughest game yet. Real Betis have been outstanding this season and put up a strong fight, but Barça finished the game relentlessly, eventually winning 5-2, making it nine wins out of nine in the domestic championship. But their dominance has also carried over to the European stage. Emphatic victories against Feyenoord and Galatasaray have set the UCL ball rolling, but now comes the biggest test of the season so far: Paris Saint-Germain. And away from home at the Parc des Princes (9pm CEST Tuesday). The French side, under the guidance of former Barça player and boss Luis Enrique, have won the last two editions of the Champions League and are once again among the hot favourites to scoops the continent's biggest prize. They too have opened the competition with back-to-back wins, and also by big margins, 6-1 over Slovan Bratislava and then 4-2 away to none other than Manchester City. But their league record has not been quite as devastating as Barça's. In an uncharacteristically poor start, they drew their first two games and then crashed to 2-1 defeat at home to Monaco. Since then it's been wins all the way, leaving them as one of five teams that are all neck-and-neck at the top of Ligue 1 with 14 points. This game has become one of the classics of European football in recent years, with a number of dramatic clashes between two sides that always be relied to play attractive football. The one everyone remembers is the famous 6-1 comeback on 2017, but in the three meetings since then it has been the Parisians who came out tops. In the 2021 round of 16, the damage was done in the first leg, which Barça lost 4-1 at home. And in 2024, despite winning the first leg in Paris, Barça then suffered another 4-1 reverse on home soil to go out in the quarter finals. And then last year, like this time in the League Phase, an early goal from Ferran Torres gave Barça an early lead, but Senny Mayulu and Gonçalo Ramos eventually earned PSG a third consecutive victory away to Barça. Ferran Torres will be involved again this year, but battling for the other side following his move to the French capital in the summer. And he's not the only former blaugrana in the visiting ranks. Current Ballon d'Or holder Ousmane Dembélé will be as huge a concern as ever, while Lucas Digne is part of what is usually regarded as the strongest rearguards in Europe. But after keeping just one clean sheet in ten games this term, questions are being asked PSG's vulnerability at the back. Rather like Barça, PSG aren't too worried about conceding goals as long as they get more at the other end. And with a squad that reads like a who's who of European football, including but not limited to Marquinhos, Vitinha, Désiré Doué, Achraf Hakimi, Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, Marquinhos and João Neves, they are a side that makes scoring goals look easy. It goes without saying that this is a massive test for the Catalans, but it's one Hansi Flick and his players are relishing. There are scores to settle with Les Rouge-et-Bleu, and this is the perfect time to do so. If winning the first 11 competitive games of the season hasn't been enough to convince anyone of Barça's immense potential this season (although it really should be), a win away to PSG would well and truly send out the message that FC Barcelona mean big business in 2026/27. In addition to the already injured Andreas Christensen and Roony Bardghji, Barça suffered the loss of two players against Betis. Jules Kounde and Eric Garcia are the new absentees. The squad announced by Hansi Flick includes 18-year-old defender Àlex Campos of Barça Atlétic, in his first ever call-up for first team duty. The big news at PSG, who rested several key players for their 3-1 win over Strasbourg at the weekend,  is the absence of Nuno Mendes. The Portuguese defender's thigh problem is not a big one, but it's big enough to keep him out of this one. The only other major doubt concerns the scorer at Spotify Camp Nou a year ago, Senny Mayulu.

title: Daniel Jones will start for Colts in Week 7 v. Vikings - Yahoo Sports
content: Daniel Jones will start at quarterback for the Indianapolis Colts in this week's game against the Minnesota Vikings. This was never truly in question, but given Jones' rocky start to the season and the Colts coming off a devastating loss to Tennessee, head coach Shane Steichen was asked on Monday if Jones would continue to be his starter. #Colts HC Shane Steichen says QB Daniel Jones will remain the team's starter against the #Vikings. DC Lou Anarumo will continue to call the defense as well. Following the Colts' loss to the Titans, Steichen reiterated his confidence in Jones, but did add that he has to clean up the turnovers. This season, Jones has thrown six interceptions -- tied for the fourth-most in the NFL -- and he's also lost a few fumbles as well. The Colts re-signed Jones in the offseason with the hope that he could regain last year's pre-injury form. However, that hasn't been the case. Jones is completing just 59% of his passes at only 5.9 yards per pass attempt, with four touchdowns and the aforementioned six interceptions. Interceptions, poor decisions, and off-target passes have been far too prevalent for Jones this season, but it's not as if conditions around him have been great. The offensive line unit struggled against the Titans, the run game has been lackluster, and without Alec Pierce, the wide receiver depth has been exposed. Jones and the 2-4 Colts will attempt to get the season back on track this week, but that won't be easy against the aggressive and blitz-heavy Vikings' defense. title: Jacob Tierney on the Secrets and Sudden Success of ‘Heated Rivalry’ - V Magazine
content: In his new book, I’ll Believe In Anything, the Heated Rivalry showrunner goes behind the scenes of a romance built on bro-ey masculinity, body language, and bold creative choices In his new book, I’ll Believe In Anything, the Heated Rivalry showrunner goes behind the scenes of a romance built on bro-ey masculinity, body language, and bold creative choices For most of the past year, the internet has been studying two hockey players’ butts and bodies on screens big and small. Lead actors Connor Storrie (as Ilya Rozanov) and Hudson Williams (as Shane Hollander) starred in some of the most-watched queer sex scenes of all time, and Jacob Tierney, the showrunner behind Heated Rivalry, made sure we could see everything the right way. The last time I spoke with him, the TV show hadn’t even premiered yet. It has since received a Peabody, a shelf full of Canadian Screen Awards, and a season-two renewal. Tierney’s new book, I’ll Believe in Anything: The Making of Heated Rivalry Season 1, is a collection of annotated scripts that reveal candid details about adapting Rachel Reid’s Game Changers series of novels to TV. The books treat sex as a character — Shane folding his clothes, Ilya’s gaze commanding a room — and so does the showrunner. “Body language is everything. Every line they say to each other until episode five is bullshit,” Tierney tells VMAN. “You have to see what they’re doing, because everything that comes out of their mouth is obfuscation. That was something we were very aware of. It’s very bro-ey, very masculine, very hockey.” He adds, “It’s not like they can’t find another guy with a great body or whatever. So this physical connection isn’t just shallow. What they reveal about themselves when they’re together, when they’re not talking, is absolutely the whole relationship.” Body language is also how gaydars beep, and how queer men cruise. “Ilya is endlessly cruising,” Tierney says. “Ilya is the one looking for connection. Ilya is a beacon. Every queer hockey player comes to Ilya. At some point, they find him, or he finds them,” within the Game Changers universe. Comparatively, Scott Hunter (François Arnaud) is the total opposite. “Scott is so afraid that his gaydar is shut off. He doesn’t want to know if anybody is gay,” Tierney teases. “Scott is in full Ken-doll, big-brother mode, you know? ‘Hi, how are you? I am Scott, I am Captain America.’” Scott and Kip (Robbie G.K.) get episode three to themselves, then a cathartic kiss on the ice rink in episode five, which has even straight men crying during watch parties. How did Tierney navigate the risk of audiences rejecting this other couple entering the narrative? Or perhaps even liking them too much, over the actual protagonists? “I knew that we were doing something structurally different with this…But I liked the idea of devoting this time to them. I thought it was cleaner,” Tierney reflects. “François freaked out. [Laughs.] He called me, and he was like, ‘The show is doing really well. They’re going to hate me!’…I was like, ‘I don’t think they will!’” Despite the show’s budget constraints, no resources are spared in preparation for the sex scenes in Heated Rivalry, which are shot as long takes with minimal coverage. “You have to do that so the audience feels permission to observe them,” Tierney says. “Seeing how one of them backs away a bit, and the other one comes forward, it tells you everything you need to know about that moment.” This makes rewatching the scenes much more interesting, too. “Watch Ilya this time,” he muses. “Next time, watch Shane.” Tierney is equally thoughtful when asked about Storrie and Williams’s naked bodies going instantly viral amid the two-episode premiere of Heated Rivalry. “The care I take is with Connor and Hudson,” he remarks. “Those are my friends. Those are my wards. I owe them a lot. We’re intertwined. Their wellbeing and safety are very important to me.” “We just had our intimacy rehearsals for season two,” he adds. “We went through all the stuff that we’re going to go through again, and we try to make sure that they’re really comfortable. They’re still so close, and they’re so game. They love these roles. They love doing it. They understood, from day one, that this is important.” Tierney admits, “I try to be very conscious that it hasn’t even been a year since this show’s been out, and they’re arguably two of the most famous people in the world. It’s fucking crazy, and there’s nothing that can prepare you for that. There’s no handbook to it. So, we just check in a lot. ‘You good?’ ‘You need anything?’” So when did he clock the scale of the Heated Rivalry phenomenon? “The HBO Golden Globes party in LA,” Tierney says. “Brendan [Brady] and I were there before Connor and Hudson arrived. And then they did, and I was like, ‘Are they the most famous people here?’” He recalls seeing a “very famous movie star awkwardly trying to figure out how to come over, and what to say.” His takeaway? “This is fucking nuts.” I’ll Believe in Anything: The Making of Heated Rivalry Season 1 is out now from Little, Brown and Company. Season two of Heated Rivalry is expected to premiere in Spring 2027. Rachel Reid’s final novel about Ilya and Shane, Unrivaled, is set for release on June 1, 2027. title: 2028 Honda CR-V: The Coming New Hybrid SUV That Could Haunt the RAV4’s Dreams - MotorTrend
content:
The next CR-V is a really big deal for Honda. Here’s what we expect from the next iteration of Honda’s bestselling compact SUV and what it may look like. No one expected the Honda CR-V to briefly become the bestselling vehicle in the country, but it happened earlier this year when the aging Honda was in the right place at the right time. That made us wonder: Could a new, redesigned CR-V grab the top spot among SUVs simply by being the best? We’ll soon find out when the new 2028 Honda CR-V debuts. Even before the 2028 CR-V arrives, reportedly sometime in early 2027, the outgoing five-seat compact SUV is already selling about as much as the Accord and Civic combined. It’s that big of a deal for Honda and the market as a whole. What you see here is our best guess at what the 2028 Honda CR-V could look like. Will Honda’s seventh-generation CR-V keep loyal buyers happy? Or will it be a regression from the outgoing SUV? Here’s what we believe we’ll see from Honda’s coming new compact SUV. The current CR-V is a solid compact SUV, but it’s no longer our favorite. Unlike the 2026 Toyota RAV4, which has gone all hybrid, the 2026–2027 CR-V still offers buyers a choice between gas and hybrid powertrains. To keep the price down, the lower trims are gas-powered, and the higher-priced trims are hybrids that generally include more features. For 2028, the CR-V is expected to go all-hybrid like the RAV4. We hope Honda will continue to offer a choice between FWD and AWD, if only to keep the base price down. We’ve already reported about how Honda’s new hybrid tech is said to be 30 percent less expensive to produce than before. That’s good considering the 2027 CR-V’s MSRP is already well above that of the Nissan Rogue, Kia Sportage, and Hyundai Tucson. The other major engineering change concerns the CR-V’s AWD system. The outgoing CR-V Hybrid uses a mechanical AWD setup, but the new model will be moving to an electric AWD approach. It’s a move that should help the 2028 CR-V better compete with the popular RAV4 in EPA-rated mileage and overall driving range. As for driving range, the RAV4 can achieve around 600 miles to a tank in a few configurations, an impressive number that the 2028 Honda CR-V Hybrid should come close to matching. We know Honda is developing its hybrid systems to be more efficient across a wider range of driving situations, which will likely mean higher highway mileage. Currently, the 2027 CR-V Hybrid sits at 40/34 mpg city/highway with AWD and 43/36 with FWD. RAV4 ratings vary by trim, but nearly every model is better than the CR-V. Perhaps not for long. The engine in the 2028 CR-V Hybrid could move to a version of Honda’s 1.5-liter turbocharged inline-four. The current hybrid uses a 2.0-liter naturally aspirated inline-four. We hope that if Honda moves to turbocharged power for the 2028 CR-V hybrid, it keeps an eye on driving smoothness. That may be just as important to some buyers as acceleration, though it must be said that the outgoing CR-V was slower in our testing than the model that came before. Honda’s Civic Hybrid offers a sublime driving experience (it uses a version of Honda’s naturally aspirated 2.0-liter at its core), so we’re crossing our fingers that the system in the new CR-V takes after that compact. Inside, the 2028 CR-V has work to do. Only a couple model years ago, Honda was still using an outdated 7.0-inch touchscreen on some CR-Vs. The outgoing model’s 9.0-inch display (pictured above) may make an appearance on lower trims, but we’re hoping the Accord’s 12.3-inch display is standard on most trims. Pairing that with the latest version of Honda’s adaptive cruise control and lane centering will go a long way toward making buyers think of the brand’s tech in a different way. Top-of-the-line 2028 CR-V Sport Tourings may also add Honda’s Sport+ feature that simulates shifts for a more connected driving experience, which debuted on the new Honda Prelude. We’ve tested it on the Prelude and haven’t been impressed so far. That trim level will be a greater value if it includes ventilated front seats and a 360 camera. Honda already offers these features in other markets on the outgoing model, so we know it’s possible. Part of what made CR-Vs so good in the past is the way they combine a spacious interior with a good driving experience and easy-to-use controls. The outgoing model was designed with physical knobs that made easy work of changing the temperature or turning down the air flow. Lately, some automakers have learned the hard way that touch-capacitive controls look tech-forward on a website but are difficult to use in person. Perhaps Honda can just skip to the part where it gives us controls that are simple to use. Another forbidden-fruit CR-V is the plug-in hybrid. Honda already offers one outside the U.S.; the real question is whether Honda will bring one here. A 2028 CR-V plug-in hybrid would allow Honda to compete directly with Toyota and its RAV4 PHEV, but it would add complexity to the lineup. Through September, PHEVs account for about 13 percent of all RAV4 sales in 2026. The 2028 CR-V should also return with a TrailSport model, though we hope this one has a more interesting interior than the outgoing SUV pictured above. Considering the Jeep Cherokee Trailhawk and Subaru Forester Wilderness, the 2028 CR-V TrailSport probably won’t be the most hardcore off-roader even within its segment, but it should offer an easier way for Honda’s more adventurous CR-V customers to head off the beaten track. Elsewhere in Honda’s lineup is the recently upgraded midsize 2027 Passport, and the Ridgeline truck returns soon, too. The truth is that unless Honda makes a steering wheel optional equipment or exclusively ships the CR-V in various shades of purple, the new 2028 model should be ubiquitous on American roads soon enough. Over time, though, that can change. That’s why it’s important that Honda doesn’t phone in the 2028 CR-V. Hyundai and Kia are making very good competing products, and the new Rogue Hybrid is one of the most impressive cars Nissan has made in years. In other words, buyers have choices. Whether the hybridized 2028 Honda CR-V remains among them will depend on how much new and improved stuff Honda adds to its bestselling SUV.
